d: OAuth 2.0 error code when the resource owner or authorization server denied the request (e.g. user clicked Deny).
OAuth 2.0 credential presented to the resource server; opaque to clients but contains or references authorization state; scoped and time-limited.

RFC 8707 resource_indicator parameter scopes the access_token to a specific target resource server URI; tokens issued without resource_indicator are general-purpose and may be accepted by any protected resource.
Integer seconds from issuance after which the access_token is no longer valid; the resource server must reject expired tokens; returned alongside access_token in the token response.
Classification of the access_token internal structure: opaque (random string referencing server-side state) or structured (JWT containing claims about scope, audience, expiration embedded directly).
OIDC id_token at_hash claim computed as base64url(left-half(SHA256(access_token))); RP verifies to confirm access_token was not tampered with.

RFC 7662 mechanism by which a resource_server POSTs the access_token to the authorization_server introspection_endpoint to determine active status, scope, expiry, and metadata before serving the protected resource.
The resource_server that receives and validates the access_token on each protected API call; the token is forwarded via HTTP Authorization header using the bearer scheme.

For opaque tokens the authorization state remains server-side; the token value is a reference (pointer) to that state rather than an encoded payload; the resource server must call introspection or validate against the authorization server to interpret the token.

A refresh_token is a long-lived credential optionally issued alongside the access_token that allows the client to obtain a new access_token without re-engaging the resource owner; the refresh_token is tied to the same scope as the original.

The specific permission set granted to the access_token; a space-delimited string drawn from the scopes requested and approved during authorization; determines what resources and actions the token authorizes.
OIDC error when prompt=select_account but the user has multiple accounts and must pick one.

The authentication context class reference actually satisfied by the OpenID Provider during an authentication event; carried in the id_token acr claim; may differ from requested_acr when best-effort matching applies.
Authentication Context Class: a statement about the authentication method used, the assurance level of the authentication event, and potentially the identity binding
Claim in the id_token containing the ACR actually used by the OP to authenticate the user, returned to the RP
The specific ACC URI returned in the acr claim of id_token, must be one of or satisfy the requested acr_values.
The URI string value that uniquely identifies a specific authentication context class; the atomic element within acr_values; examples drawn from SAML ACR URN namespace.

OIDC parameter flag accompanying acr_values indicating whether the requested ACR is required (essential=true) or preferred; when essential=true and no acceptable ACR can be satisfied the OP returns an error.
The 'acr' claim embedded in the signed id_token; carries the achieved_acr identifier as a URI string; RP inspects this to verify authentication context requirements were met.
The determination by the OP of which requested ACR (if any) was satisfied by the authentication performed; evaluated against the ordered acr_values list in priority order; result is the achieved_acr.
Identity provider condition when no requested ACC in acr_values can be satisfied, causing authentication failure per prompt=none semantics.

The algorithmic step the OP performs upon receiving acr_values: iterate the ordered list, evaluate each acr_class against the authentication that will be performed, return the first satisfied class as achieved_acr in the id_token.
The subset of an OIDC Authorization Request that specifies acr_values (and optionally acr_values essential flag); the structured representation of the RP's authentication context requirements.
A requirement statement specifying which ACRs the RP considers acceptable and in what priority order
The OP evaluating its authentication mechanisms against the requested ACRs and determining which ones it can satisfy
The internal OP policy defining how ordered acr_values list is processed to select the achieved_acr; typically returns the first class in the list that the authentication event satisfied.
OIDC authentication context class reference values requested by RP; ordered list the OP attempts to satisfy (e.g. 'urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:Password').

The conceptual distinction that acr addresses authentication context class (what kind of assurance) while AMR addresses authentication method (how the user proved identity); acr is coarse-grained context, AMR is fine-grained mechanism.

A named authentication context class identified by a URI string; represents a defined level of assurance or authentication method category that an Identity Provider can declare it satisfied in an authentication event.
Level of Assurance semantics governing the ordering of ACC URIs in acr_values; higher-positioned ACCs imply stronger authentication requirements.

The AMR claim in id_token listing specific authentication methods used (e.g. OTP, swk); distinct from acr which addresses context class; both may coexist in id_token to fully characterize the authentication event.
Short-lived credential exchanged for tokens at the token endpoint; exists to keep tokens out of the user-agent (browser) history and address bar.
Primary OAuth 2.0 flow for web apps with a server-side component; uses authorization_endpoint then token_endpoint with the returned code.
Threat where malware or network attacker steals the authorization code from the browser redirect; mitigated by PKCE requiring proof at token time.
OAuth 2.0 endpoint where the resource owner authenticates and grants consent; returns authorization_code via redirect or form_post response.
OAuth 2.0 server that authenticates the resource owner, obtains consent, and issues access tokens and optionally refresh tokens and ID tokens.
RFC 8414 metadata document at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server; lists server capabilities, endpoint URLs, grant types, and supported features.
OAuth 2.0 authorization code: a short-lived, single-use opaque credential issued by the authorization_endpoint and exchanged at the token_endpoint for access_token and optional refresh_token.
OIDC Logout spec using direct server-to-server POST to RP logout endpoint; more reliable than front-channel but requires RP endpoint.
Token type defined in RFC 6750; any party possessing the token may use it; security relies on transport TLS and token secrecy.

RFC 6750 token type specifying that possession of the access_token is sufficient proof of authorization; the token is transmitted in the Authorization header as 'Bearer <token>' or in body/form when headers are unavailable.
Identity provider selection rule: when acr_values lists multiple ACCs ordered by LoA, OP returns the highest ACC it can satisfy rather than failing.
OIDC RP iframe that polls the OP to detect changes in login state (e.g. user logged out elsewhere); enables cross-tab session sync.
RFC 9002 Client Initiated Backchannel Authentication; user initiates auth from a device, push notification is sent to their phone, RP polls for result.
OIDC parameter requesting specific claims in id_token or userinfo response; server may return subset based on policy and user consent.
Identity provider rule set determining which claims can be released to a given relying_party based on client registration, user consent records, and data availability.
Structured JSON object within the claims parameter containing claim preferences for id_token and userinfo endpoints; root container for granular claim directives.
Discovery metadata field listing which claims the OP is capable of returning; clients use it to check support before requesting.
Relying party validation that returned claims match what was requested in the claims_parameter, checking essential claims are present and values satisfy policy constraints.
Application making protected resource requests on behalf of the resource owner; classified as confidential (can hold secrets) or public (cannot).
JWT used for client authentication at the token_endpoint; signed with client's private key; contains iss, sub, aud, exp, jti claims.
OAuth 2.0 flow where the client authenticates with its own credentials and receives an access token representing the client itself (no user).
Public identifier assigned by the authorization server to a client; used to identify which application is requesting authorization.
Confidential credential held by the client; used with authorization_code or client_credentials flows to authenticate the client to the token endpoint.
OIDC acr_values requested during authorization and stored with the code so the token endpoint can confirm the authentication context was satisfied.
The target resource or client_id for which the authorization code was issued; determines the audience claim in the resulting access_token.
The redirect_uri parameter value carried in the original authorization request and bound to the authorization_code; must match exactly at token_endpoint exchange to prevent redirection hijacking.
PKCE challenge derived from code_verifier; method S256 sends base64url(SHA256(code_verifier)); method plain sends verifier as-is.
PKCE parameter specifying how code_challenge was computed: S256 (SHA256 hash) or plain (plaintext); server uses same to verify.
OIDC claims_parameter values requested at authorization and preserved with the code so the userinfo endpoint or id_token reflects them.
The authorization code is bound to the client_id that initiated the flow; the token request must authenticate as that same client using client_secret or DPoP proof.
Timestamp when token_endpoint successfully exchanged the authorization_code; after consumption the code becomes invalid and cannot be reused.
Integer seconds after code_issued_at during which the authorization_code remains valid; short-lived by design to limit interception window; typically 60 seconds.
The brief time window (typically 60 seconds) after which the authorization_code becomes invalid if not exchanged; short lifetime limits interception exposure.
Server-defined structure encoding issuer, client_id, expiry, nonce, scope, and optionally the actual token claims; format is opaque to the client and may be a signed JWT.
OIDC id_token c_hash claim; analogous to at_hash but for authorization_code; verified when hybrid flow returns code from authorization_endpoint.
RFC 7662 introspection response for a code used at the token endpoint reveals its active status, expiry, scope, and client_id before the exchange completes.
Timestamp when authorization_server generated the authorization_code; used to enforce short-lived code_expires_in window for security.
The client_id identifying which registered client the authorization_code was issued to; enforced at token_endpoint exchange.
The authorization_server entity that generates and later validates the authorization_code at token exchange.

OIDC RFC 7519 nonce parameter sent in the authorization request for implicit/hybrid flows; bound to the authorization_code so the id_token returned at token_endpoint can be correlated to the original auth request.
When PKCE is active the authorization code is bound to the code_challenge presented during the authorization request; the token request must present the matching code_verifier.
The challenge derived from code_verifier and sent to authorization_endpoint during authorization request; authorization_server stores this to validate later code exchange.
The high-entropy random string (code_verifier from PKCE) required at token_endpoint to redeem authorization_code when PKCE was used in authorization request.
The pre-registered redirect_uri to which authorization_server sends the authorization_code via browser redirect; must exactly match client registration.
The redirect_uri parameter is bound to the authorization code at issuance; the redirect URI used during token exchange must match the registered URI.
The resource_indicator URI specified in the authorization request and attached to the authorization_code; scopes the issued access_token to that specific resource server.
The scope value string authorized by the resource owner and attached to the authorization_code; governs what access_token scope can be granted at token exchange.
The server-enforced property that each authorization code may be presented exactly once; a second exchange attempt returns invalid_grant.
The opaque state parameter echoed back by authorization_server to client via redirect_uri; client validates state matches its original value to prevent CSRF attacks.

The state parameter value echoed by the authorization_server from the authorization request; client validates it in the redirect response to confirm the authorization session integrity and mitigate CSRF.
The opaque string value of the authorization_code itself; a high-entropy random token generated by the authorization_server.
The raw string credential itself; opaque to the client; server-side only; base64url-encoded per implementation.
PKCE random string (43-128 chars) kept secret by the client and sent hashed as code_challenge at authorization request time.
OAuth 2.0 client capable of securely maintaining a client_secret (web server applications); can authenticate at the token_endpoint.
Cross-site request forgery threat against OAuth authorization callback; mitigated by the state parameter binding request and response.
RFC 8628 OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant; user enters a code on a separate device while the client polls for authorization completion.
Well-known URL pattern (RFC 5785) at /.well-known/openid-configuration exposing OIDC provider configuration JSON.
RFC 9449 Demonstrated Proof-of-Possession; client signs a JWT with its private key and includes DPoP header in token requests to bind the token to the key.
OIDC endpoint the RP redirects the user to for logout; OP invalidates session cookie and may trigger front-channel or back-channel logout to other RPs.
Claim marked as required by the relying party; identity provider must return this claim or return an error satisfying the acr_values if unable to fulfill.
Integer seconds indicating access token lifetime; returned alongside access_token in token response.
Multi-domain identity arrangement where one identity_provider serves multiple relying_parties across organizational boundaries; uses OIDC or SAML.
OIDC response mode where authorization response parameters are encoded in an auto-submitted HTML form POST to the redirect_uri.
OIDC Logout spec using hidden iframes to notify RPs that a user logged out; RP renders a front-channel logout iframe.
OAuth 2.0 parameter identifying which authorization flow is being used; values: authorization_code, client_credentials, refresh_token, password (deprecated).
OIDC flow variant returning id_token and/or authorization_code from authorization_endpoint (front channel) while also allowing token_endpoint exchange.
OIDC JWT containing subject identifier (sub), issuer, audience, expiration, authentication event metadata, and optionally user claims; always signed.
Claims section of claims_request specifying which claims the relying party wants embedded directly in the signed id_token JWT.
OIDC parameter carrying a previously issued id_token; OP uses it to infer the user and potentially skip re-authentication or pre-fill consent.
OIDC term for the authorization server that also acts as the authentication authority; issues id_token and exposes userinfo.
Historical OIDC flow returning access_token via fragment; removed from OIDC Core due to token exposure in browser history and lack of PKCE equivalent.
OIDC error when the authorization request requires an interaction the user is not currently engaged in (prompt=none failure).
RFC 7662 endpoint allowing resource servers to validate access tokens; returns active status, scope, expiry, and other token metadata.
OAuth 2.0 error code when client authentication fails at the token_endpoint (unknown client_id, wrong secret, revoked credentials).
OAuth 2.0 error code when the provided authorization grant or refresh token is invalid, expired, revoked, or already used.
OAuth 2.0 error code for missing, malformed, or invalid parameters in the authorization request.
OAuth 2.0 error code when the requested scope is invalid, unknown, or exceeds what was originally granted.
String identifier (typically URL) in id_token and access_token; relying parties validate tokens were issued by a trusted, matching issuer.
RFC 7517 JSON Web Key; JSON representation of a cryptographic key (RSA, EC, Oct) with kty, use, alg, n, e or crv fields.
RFC 7517 JWK Set; JSON object with 'keys' array containing JWK entries; served at jwks_uri for token signature verification.
Shorthand for JWK Set; the JSON payload served at the jwks_uri endpoint containing the public keys for verifying ID tokens and access tokens.
URL in discovery document pointing to JSON Web Key Set (RFC 7517) containing public keys used to verify id_token and access_token signatures.
RFC 7519 JSON Web Token; base64url-encoded JSON envelope containing claims; can be signed (JWS) or encrypted (JWE); id_token is always a JWS.
LoA: an assurance level (e.g., LoA1 through LoA4) that classifies the strength of authentication; ACRs often map to LoA
OIDC parameter suggesting which account the user should log in with; may be email, username, or account selector hint.
OIDC error when prompt=none but the user is not currently authenticated and must log in.
OIDC parameter specifying maximum seconds since last authentication; if elapsed, OP must re-authenticate before issuing id_token.
Threat where an attacker substitutes the authorization server's issuer identifier causing the client to send tokens to the wrong server.
Mobile or desktop OAuth 2.0 public client; uses PKCE; may use app linking (claimed https redirect_uri) or custom scheme (e.g. com.app://oauth).
OIDC string value transmitted in authorization request, embedded in id_token, and validated by the relying party to prevent replay attacks.

IETF RFC 6749 authorization framework enabling third-party application access to protected resources without sharing credentials; defines four grant types and token issuance via authorization and token endpoints.
Identity provider algorithm matching requested acr_values against supported authentication methods to determine which ACC to satisfy or whether to error.
Security vulnerability where the authorization server redirects to a URI not matching the registered redirect_uri; mitigated by exact string matching.
Discovery document served at /.well-known/openid-configuration; machine-readable metadata listing endpoints, supported features, and server capabilities.
Identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 (OIDC 1.0, OIDC Core spec) adding ID tokens as JWTs, userinfo endpoint, and standardized identity claims for authentication use cases.
OIDC subject identifier strategy where each RP receives a different sub for the same user, preventing cross-RP user correlation.
Pushed Authorization Request endpoint; requires client authentication; returns request_uri valid for a short window (e.g. 60 seconds).
Server response state where only a subset of requested claims are returned; occurs when policy or consent excludes some claims from the request.
RFC 7636 Proof Key for Code Exchange; mitigates authorization code interception by requiring code_verifier and code_challenge from the client.
OIDC parameter controlling user interaction: none (no prompt, error if needed), login (force re-auth), consent (show approval screen), select_account.
OAuth 2.0 client unable to securely store a client_secret; mobile apps, SPAs; always uses PKCE; cannot use client_secret_post or client_secret_basic.
OIDC subject identifier strategy where the same sub is issued to all RPs; used for cases where cross-RP identity sharing is desired.
RFC 9126 PAR: client POSTs authorization request parameters to par_endpoint first, receives request_uri for use at authorization_endpoint.
Callback URL the authorization server redirects to after consent; must be pre-registered with the authorization server and must match exactly.
OAuth 2.0 credential used to obtain new access tokens without re-prompting the resource owner; long-lived and tied to the same scope as the original access token.
Security practice where each refresh token use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one; detects token theft via reuse.
OIDC term for the client application that relies on the identity provider's id_token for user authentication.
RFC 9101 JAR: a signed and optionally encrypted JWT containing authorization request parameters; either passed inline or via request_uri.
OIDC/JAR parameter referencing an external request_uri hosting the request_object; server fetches and processes it before consent.
The authentication context class reference(s) carried in the acr_request that the RP prefers or requires for the authentication event being initiated.
RFC 8707 parameter specifying the target resource server URI; server issues access token scoped to that specific resource, not just the general API.
Entity capable of granting access to a protected resource; typically the end-user who authenticates to authorize the client's request.
Server hosting protected resources; validates incoming access tokens and returns resources only when tokens are valid and authorized.
RFC 7009 endpoint allowing clients to invalidate refresh or access tokens; supports bearer tokens and is advisory (server may retain copy).
Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0; XML-based SSO protocol predating OIDC; OIDC was designed to provide similar functionality with JSON and REST.
SAML 2.0 authentication context class URIs (urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:*) used for OIDC-to-SAML federation interoperability in acr_values.
SAML authentication context class identifier URIs reused as OIDC ACR values (e.g., urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:Password)
OAuth 2.0 mechanism for requesting specific permission sets; space-delimited string (e.g. 'openid profile email'); server grants subset based on policy.
OIDC mechanism for grouping redirect_uris under one sector identifier; used to derive pairwise subject identifiers from a separate sector host.
OAuth 2.0 error code (error=server_error) when the authorization server encounters an unexpected condition preventing request fulfillment.
JWS: a JWT with a JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515); id_token is typically a signed JWT using RS256 or ES256 algorithm.
Single Page Application: browser-based public client using PKCE; historically used implicit flow, now encouraged toward authorization_code + PKCE with no secret.
OIDC defined claims set (name, email, phone, address, birthdate, gender, picture, website) in OIDC Core Section 5.1.
OAuth 2.0 CSRF protection parameter; opaque string generated by the client, echoed back in the callback, and validated for binding the request and response.
The 'sub' claim in id_token: a unique stable identifier assigned by the identity provider to the user; pairwise vs public based on RP.
Cryptographic binding of tokens to the TLS channel or a key; id_token is bound to the channel used during the authorization request.
OAuth 2.0 endpoint accepting authorization_code or other grants and returning access_token, refresh_token, and optional id_token.
Metadata field specifying how the client authenticates at the token_endpoint: client_secret_basic, client_secret_post, private_key_jwt, none.
The HTTP response from the token_endpoint containing the access_token plus optionally refresh_token, expires_in, scope, and token_type as JSON members.
RFC 8693 Token Exchange grant; allows a client to exchange one token type for another (e.g. exchange a refresh token for an audience-scoped access token).
RFC 7662 introspection: protected endpoint where resource servers POST access_token to get its status, scope, expiration, and active flag.
Exposure of access_token or refresh_token to unauthorized parties via logs, browser history, or insecure storage; mitigated by transport security and short-lived tokens.
Refresh token rotation mechanism detecting replay: if the same refresh token is used twice, the server revokes the entire token family.
OAuth 2.0 parameter indicating how the access_token is to be presented to the resource server, typically Bearer, specifying the authorization scheme to use in requests.
OAuth 2.0 hint parameter in refresh requests indicating whether the token being refreshed is an access_token or refresh_token.
OIDC parameter indicating user's preferred languages for the consent/userinfo UI; BCP 47 language tag list.
OAuth 2.0 error code when the client is not authorized to use the requested grant_type (not registered or policy forbids it).
OAuth 2.0 error code when the grant_type is not supported by the authorization server.
End-user authorization for the identity provider to release specific claims; may be granted, denied, or limited compared to what relying party requested.
Claims section of claims_request specifying which claims the relying party wants returned from the userinfo_endpoint after token exchange.
OIDC protected endpoint returning user claims as a JSON object; called with access_token after successful authentication; claims may overlap with id_token.
Claim requested by the relying party but not mandated; identity provider may omit based on policy, user consent, or availability without error.
OIDC silent authentication using id_token_hint or session cookie to authenticate without explicit user interaction when prompt=none.
